title: Opener Wins the End-Pick Game
statement:
A row of cards lies on the table; card i is worth nums[i] points. Two players take turns, and the opener moves first. On each turn a player takes one card from either end of the row and adds its points to their own total. The game ends when the row is empty.

Both players play perfectly to maximise their own total. Return true if the opener ends with at least as many points as the other player (a tie counts as a win for the opener), otherwise false.

examples.why: Whichever end the opener takes, the 9 is exposed and the other player grabs it: 5 against 9.
The opener ends with 2 + 2 = 4 and the other player with 4. A tie is a win for the opener.
Taking 4 first lets the opener also take the 8 later: 12 against 4.

hints: Taking the larger end card is not always right: it may expose a big card to the other player. You need to look ahead.
Score the game as a single number: the mover's total minus the other player's total, for the cards still left. The opener wins if that number is at least 0 for the whole row.

Let best(i, j) be that difference for the cards i..j. Taking the left card gives nums[i] − best(i + 1, j), taking the right gives nums[j] − best(i, j − 1). Fill the table from short ranges to long ones.

explain.intuition:
Track only one number: how far ahead the player to move can get on the cards that are left. After you take a card, the roles swap, and your opponent's lead on the rest counts against you. So for the cards i..j, your best lead is the larger of nums[i] − best(i+1, j) and nums[j] − best(i, j−1).

That recursion has only O(n²) distinct ranges, so a table filled from short ranges up turns an exponential game tree into a quadratic loop. The opener wins exactly when best(0, n−1) ≥ 0.
steps: Let dp[j] hold the best lead on the range i..j for the current start i.
Go through i from the last index down to 0, and set dp[i] = nums[i] (one card: you take it).
For each j > i, set dp[j] = max(nums[i] − dp[j], nums[j] − dp[j − 1]). The old dp[j] is the range i+1..j; the fresh dp[j − 1] is i..j−1.
pitfalls: Playing greedily by taking the bigger end. In [2, 9, 3] taking the 3 still hands the 9 to the other player; you have to look at what each move exposes.
Returning dp[n − 1] > 0. A tie counts as a win for the opener.
Tracking both players' totals separately in the recursion. The difference alone is enough, and it keeps the state to two indexes.

solutions.title: Plain game-tree recursion
solutions.idea: Try both ends at every turn and keep the better lead for the mover. Correct, but it explores 2ⁿ move sequences.

solutions.title: Interval table in one row
solutions.idea: The lead on i..j depends only on i+1..j and i..j−1. Sweep i downwards and keep a single row of leads.

followups: Show that with an even number of cards the opener can never lose. What simple strategy guarantees it?
Return the opener's final total instead of a yes or no. What changes in the table?
